parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 13. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man called Oliver phoning the secretary of a local history society. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. Margaret: Hello, Margaret Hay speaking. Oliver: Oh, hello. My name's Oliver Grant. I got your number from the notice in the library. I've just moved to Ashbrook, and I'm interested in joining the local history society. Margaret: That's wonderful. We're always looking for new members. What would you like to know? Oliver: Well, I'd like to know what kind of things you do on a regular basis. Margaret: OK. Well, one of our main activities is looking after our archive. That's in the basement of the library. People have given us all sorts of things over the years, letters, maps, school reports, and at the moment we're sorting and labelling a big collection of old photographs that were found in the attic of a house on the High Street. Oliver: That sounds fascinating. I used to work in a museum, so I've done that kind of thing before. Margaret: Oh, that's very useful. You'll know the rules, then. Some of the documents are quite fragile, so no pens are allowed in the archive room. We only use pencils. Oliver: Yes, that's quite normal. What about food and drink? Margaret: Well, we don't eat in there, obviously, but there's a little kitchen next door where we have a cup of tea. Oliver: Fine. And do you do anything apart from the archive? Margaret: Yes. We've got an oral history project, where we record interviews with some of the older residents about their memories of the town. Last year we talked to people who had worked on the farms around here, and the next group we'd like to talk to is people who used to work at the old brewery. It closed in the nineteen eighties, but it was the biggest employer in Ashbrook for over a century. Oliver: I'd love to help with that. Margaret: Great. We've also got a small group who are researching the history of local pubs. There used to be over twenty in the town, and some of them had quite a colourful history. Oliver: I can imagine. Is there anything else? Margaret: Well, our big project at the moment is for our website. We already have a timeline of the town's history on there, and now we're creating a map that shows where all the old buildings used to stand, with photos of each one. People can click on a building and see what it looked like a hundred years ago. Oliver: That's a great idea. And how often do members meet? Margaret: We have a meeting on the first Tuesday of every month, usually with a guest speaker. Last month, someone came to talk about the Roman road that runs just north of the town. Oliver: Really? I didn't know there was one. Margaret: Not many people do. Most of it is under farmland now, but you can still see a short section near the golf course. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Margaret: Now, we've also got a couple of events coming up that might interest you. On Saturday, we're having a guided walk. It's open to everyone, not just members. Oliver: Where does it start? Margaret: We usually meet at the church, but this time we're meeting outside the town hall, at ten o'clock. Then we'll walk along the old canal, which is a lovely route, and finish at the quarry. It was where most of the stone for the town's buildings came from, and one of our members is going to explain how it was cut and transported. Oliver: How long is the walk? Margaret: It's about eight kilometres there and back, so you'll need good shoes. And one other thing: bring a torch, because part of the route goes through an old tunnel under the railway, and there's no lighting in it. Oliver: OK. I'll remember that. Do I need to bring lunch? Margaret: No, we'll stop at a pub on the way back. Oliver: Great. I'll definitely come. You mentioned a couple of events. Margaret: Yes, the other is a workshop on family history. Lots of people want to find out about their ancestors but don't know where to start. So one of our members, who's a professional researcher, is going to show people how to use online census records. They're one of the most useful sources, because they tell you who was living in each house, and what their jobs were. Oliver: I've always wanted to do that. When is it? Margaret: It's on the twelfth of next month, from two until five, in the library. Oliver: And is there a charge? Margaret: It's free for members. For non-members it's normally twelve pounds, but we've managed to reduce it this time, so it's just eight pounds, and that includes tea and cake. Oliver: That's very reasonable. Well, I think I'd like to join anyway, so I'd get in for free. How much is membership? Margaret: It's fifteen pounds a year. I can send you a form by email if you give me your address. Oliver: Thanks. It's oliver dot grant at mailbox dot com. Margaret: Lovely. I'll send it this evening. And hopefully I'll see you on Saturday. Oliver: You will. Thanks very much, Margaret. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide called Fiona speaking to a group of passengers at the start of a trip on a heritage steam railway. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome aboard the Glen Arran Steam Railway. My name's Fiona, and I'll be your guide for today's journey. The trip to Carrick and back takes about three hours, and I'll be telling you about some of the things you can see along the way. But first, a little history. Many people assume that this line was built for tourists, or to carry fish from the coast, but in fact it was built in the eighteen seventies to transport slate from the quarries in the hills down to the harbour. Passengers were only carried later, and the line closed completely in nineteen sixty-four. It was reopened by volunteers in the nineteen nineties. Guide: Now, a few practical points. The train has five carriages. Right behind the engine is the observation car, which has large windows on three sides. The second and third carriages are standard ones, and the fourth has tables and a buffet counter, if you'd like to play cards or do a crossword. We've kept the last carriage for families with young children, as it's nearest to the guard's van, and there's more space for pushchairs. Guide: You may have noticed that the buffet counter is closed today, I'm afraid. We're waiting for a part for the water heater. But don't worry, one of our volunteers will be coming round with a trolley selling hot drinks and snacks, so you won't go thirsty. The station café is open when we get back, too. Guide: Lots of you will want to take photographs, and you're very welcome to. But please don't lean out of the windows, as there are places where the branches come very close to the train. The best place for photos is the observation car at the front of the train. It can get quite crowded, so please take turns in there. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: About twenty minutes into the journey, we'll cross the Arran Viaduct, which is the highlight of the trip for most people. People always ask me who designed it, and to be honest, nobody's quite sure. The records were lost when the railway company's offices burned down. What we do know is why it's built on a curve. The engineers needed to avoid a stretch of very soft ground at the bottom of the valley, so they bent the line around it. The other thing people are often surprised by is that it's made of concrete, not stone. It was one of the first large concrete structures in the country, and it's lasted remarkably well. It's forty metres high at its highest point, so if you don't like heights, you might want to look the other way. Guide: After the viaduct, we'll be travelling through some of the wildest countryside in Scotland, so keep your eyes open. You're very likely to see golden eagles over the hills on the left, as there's a pair nesting nearby. Red deer are often seen from the train in spring, but at this time of year they stay high up in the mountains, so you're unlikely to see any today. When we run alongside the river, look out for otters. They're shy, but they don't seem to mind the train at all, and passengers see them on most trips. Ospreys also used to nest by the loch, but they've already left for Africa for the winter. And although there are pine martens in the forest, they only come out at night. Guide: At the end of the line, we'll stop at Carrick Halt before the engine is turned round for the return journey. There's a café there in the summer, but it's already closed for the winter, so if you'd like something to eat, make sure you buy it from the trolley. There used to be a small museum as well, but it's been moved to our main station, so you can see it when we get back. Some people ask if they can walk to the waterfall from Carrick, but it's too far to get there and back in the time we have. The train will only wait for twenty minutes, so please make sure you're back on board by then, because we can't wait for anyone who's late. And please note that the toilets at Carrick are the only ones on the route, as those on the train are out of order today. Right, I think we're about to leave, so sit back and enjoy the journey. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two archaeology students, Ella and Ravi, discussing their summer excavation placements and their course modules. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Ella: Hi, Ravi. How was your summer? You were on a dig, weren't you? Ravi: Yes, I spent four weeks on an excavation in Yorkshire. It was brilliant, although it took me ages to get a place. I must have emailed about ten different projects, and most of them never even replied. Ella: That happened to me too. I think the people running them are just so busy in the summer that they don't have time to answer emails. In the end, my tutor phoned someone she knew, and I got a place straight away. Ravi: Lucky you. At least the cost wasn't a problem for me. The project paid for my accommodation, and I got a lift there with another student. Ella: Same here. And four weeks was just the right length. So what did you find? Ravi: Well, mostly bits of animal bone and some very ordinary pottery. I was hoping to find a coin, but no one on the whole site found one. But on my last week I found a small piece of a pot with a few letters scratched into it. The director thought it might be part of the owner's name. I was so pleased, I think I talked about it for days. Ella: That's amazing. I didn't find anything as exciting as that. My site was on the edge of a town, and it was being excavated because a supermarket is going to be built there. So we had to work quite fast, before the builders moved in. Ravi: Had anyone dug there before? Ella: No, nobody knew there was anything there until a survey was done for the planning application. Everyone thought it was just an old farm field. Ravi: So what did you find in the end? Ella: The remains of a Roman house, with part of a mosaic floor. The developers have agreed to change their plans slightly, so that it can be preserved under the car park. Ravi: Interesting. What did you think about the way they recorded the finds? I was surprised how strict they were. Ella: So was I. I'd assumed that taking photographs was enough, but they still wanted drawings as well. And they were very clear that you must record the exact position of an object before you lift it out of the ground. Once it's moved, that information is lost for ever. Ravi: Yes, my supervisor said exactly the same thing. Did you do any finds washing? Ella: Oh, don't remind me. I did something really stupid. I was given a tray of finds to wash, and I didn't read the label properly. It said that some of the seeds in it were burnt and mustn't be washed, because they were going to be sent to a lab. I washed the lot. Luckily, there were plenty more samples. Ravi: Oh no. Well, at least you didn't break anything. Did your supervisor say anything about volunteers? Mine had some strong views on that. Ella: Mine too. She said that a lot of the work they pay specialists to do, like sorting pottery, could easily be done by volunteers with a bit of guidance. Ravi: That's exactly what my supervisor said. She thought there were plenty of volunteers, but they weren't being given enough responsibility. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Ella: Anyway, we need to choose our modules for next year. What did you think of the ones we did last term? Ravi: Well, I was dreading the dating techniques module, because there was so much chemistry involved. But actually, once the lecturer explained how radiocarbon dating works, it all made sense, and I got a good mark in the exam. Ella: I found the reading for that one really heavy going, though. All those chapters on tree rings. What about human remains? Ravi: That was the one that really affected me. I had no idea how many skeletons from medieval cemeteries show signs of serious injury. Nearly all the adults seemed to have broken bones. I found that quite disturbing. Ella: Yes, it certainly makes you realise how hard life was. And ancient trade? Ravi: That was interesting, but what struck me was how many basic questions haven't been answered yet. Ella: I felt exactly the same. We know goods like amber travelled right across Europe, but nobody really knows how, or who was carrying them. I was amazed there's so little research on it. Ravi: And what about underwater archaeology? You seemed to love that. Ella: I did. The lectures weren't very well organised, and the reading list was far too long, but I've already started looking at master's courses in it. I'd really like to learn to dive and work on shipwrecks. Ravi: Well, you'd better start swimming lessons, then. Ella: Very funny. Actually, I'm quite a good swimmer. Anyway, shall we meet on Friday and go through the options for next year together? Ravi: Good idea. I'll bring the course handbook, and we can make a list. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student giving a presentation on the history of kites. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation today, I'm going to talk about kites. Most of us think of them as toys, something you fly on the beach on a windy afternoon. But kites have a long and surprisingly serious history, and they've played a part in science, warfare and religion in many parts of the world. I became interested in the subject last year, when I visited a kite museum in Japan and was amazed by how many different traditions there are. Student: Kites were almost certainly first made in China, over two thousand years ago. According to tradition, the very first ones were made of wood, but they soon came to be made from silk stretched over a frame of bamboo, both of which were widely available in China. And they weren't used for fun. The military used them to send signals between groups of soldiers, and there are even stories of kites being used to measure the distance to an enemy's walls. In some parts of Indonesia, a very different tradition developed. There, kites were made from leaves, and fishermen flew them over the sea with a line and bait hanging down into the water. This method is still used today in some places, and some researchers believe the tradition may be even older than the Chinese one, although there is little evidence to prove it. Student: Kites also played an important role in the history of science. The most famous example is probably Benjamin Franklin, who in seventeen fifty-two is said to have flown a kite in a thunderstorm to show that lightning was a form of electricity. It was a very dangerous thing to do, and some later scientists who tried to repeat it were killed. Historians still argue about whether Franklin really carried out the experiment in the way he described. At the end of the nineteenth century, an Australian inventor called Lawrence Hargrave developed the box kite, which was much more stable than earlier designs. He even lifted himself off the ground using four of them tied together. A few years later, the Wright brothers used kites to test their ideas about the design of wings, before they built their first powered aircraft. And for about forty years, weather services in several countries used kites to carry instruments high into the sky, to measure the air temperature and the speed of the wind. This continued until aircraft and balloons took over the job in the nineteen thirties. Student: Kites are also an important part of many cultures. In the Indian state of Gujarat, a huge kite festival is held every January to mark the end of winter. It lasts two days, and many families spend almost the whole time on their rooftops. In recent years, it has also attracted visitors from all over the world. The sky over cities like Ahmedabad is filled with kites, and people compete to cut each other's strings. To make this possible, the strings are coated with a mixture of glue and powdered glass. Sadly, this causes many injuries to birds, and in some places the most dangerous types of string have now been banned. Student: In Guatemala, on the first of November, people in some towns fly enormous, brightly coloured kites in the cemeteries. Some of these are several metres across, and they can take months to make. Their designs often include messages about social issues, as well as traditional patterns. The kites are believed to carry messages to the dead, and to help families feel close to relatives they have lost. Student: Finally, kites can have political meaning too. In Afghanistan, kite flying has been a popular pastime for centuries, and kite fighting is a traditional sport. As in India, the aim is to cut your opponent's string, and children race through the streets to catch the kites that have been cut loose. But during the years when the Taliban were in power in the late nineteen nineties, kite flying was banned, along with many other forms of entertainment. When that period ended, one of the first things people did was fly their kites again. Many people know this story from the novel The Kite Runner. So, as you can see, kites are much more than toys. In the second part of my talk, I'd like to look at how they're being used today, including some recent experiments using kites to generate electricity. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

Well, I think I'd like to join anyway, so I'd get in for free. How much is membership? Margaret: It's fifteen pounds a year. I can send you a form by email if you give me your address. Oliver: Thanks. It's oliver dot grant at mailbox dot com. Margaret: Lovely. I'll send it this evening. And hopefully I'll see you on Saturday. Oliver: You will. Thanks very much, Margaret. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide called Fiona speaking to a group of passengers at the start of a trip on a heritage steam railway. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome aboard the Glen Arran Steam Railway. My name's Fiona, and I'll be your guide for today's journey. The trip to Carrick and back takes about three hours, and I'll be telling you about some of the things you can see along the way. But first, a little history. Many people assume that this line was built for tourists, or to carry fish from the coast, but in fact it was built in the eighteen seventies to transport slate from the quarries in the hills down to the harbour. Passengers were only carried later, and the line closed completely in nineteen sixty-four. It was reopened by volunteers in the nineteen nineties. Guide: Now, a few practical points. The train has five carriages. Right behind the engine is the observation car, which has large windows on three sides. The second and third carriages are standard ones, and the fourth has tables and a buffet counter, if you'd like to play cards or do a crossword. We've kept the last carriage for families with young children, as it's nearest to the guard's van, and there's more space for pushchairs. Guide: You may have noticed that the buffet counter is closed today, I'm afraid. We're waiting for a part for the water heater. But don't worry, one of our volunteers will be coming round with a trolley selling hot drinks and snacks, so you won't go thirsty. The station café is open when we get back, too. Guide: Lots of you will want to take photographs, and you're very welcome to. But please don't lean out of the windows, as there are places where the branches come very close to the train. The best place for photos is the observation car at the front of the train. It can get quite crowded, so please take turns in there. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: About twenty minutes into the journey, we'll cross the Arran Viaduct, which is the highlight of the trip for most people. People always ask me who designed it, and to be honest, nobody's quite sure. The records were lost when the railway company's offices burned down. What we do know is why it's built on a curve. The engineers needed to avoid a stretch of very soft ground at the bottom of the valley, so they bent the line around it. The other thing people are often surprised by is that it's made of concrete, not stone. It was one of the first large concrete structures in the country, and it's lasted remarkably well. It's forty metres high at its highest point, so if you don't like heights, you might want to look the other way. Guide: After the viaduct, we'll be travelling through some of the wildest countryside in Scotland, so keep your eyes open. You're very likely to see golden eagles over the hills on the left, as there's a pair nesting nearby. Red deer are often seen from the train in spring, but at this time of year they stay high up in the mountains, so you're unlikely to see any today. When we run alongside the river, look out for otters. They're shy, but they don't seem to mind the train at all, and passengers see them on most trips. Ospreys also used to nest by the loch, but they've already left for Africa for the winter. And although there are pine martens in the forest, they only come out at night. Guide: At the end of the line, we'll stop at Carrick Halt before the engine is turned round for the return journey. There's a café there in the summer, but it's already closed for the winter, so if you'd like something to eat, make sure you buy it from the trolley. There used to be a small museum as well, but it's been moved to our main station, so you can see it when we get back. Some people ask if they can walk to the waterfall from Carrick, but it's too far to get there and back in the time we have. The train will only wait for twenty minutes, so please make sure you're back on board by then, because we can't wait for anyone who's late. And please note that the toilets at Carrick are the only ones on the route, as those on the train are out of order today. Right, I think we're about to leave, so sit back and enjoy the journey. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two archaeology students, Ella and Ravi, discussing their summer excavation placements and their course modules. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Ella: Hi, Ravi. How was your summer? You were on a dig, weren't you? Ravi: Yes, I spent four weeks on an excavation in Yorkshire. It was brilliant, although it took me ages to get a place. I must have emailed about ten different projects, and most of them never even replied. Ella: That happened to me too. I think the people running them are just so busy in the summer that they don't have time to answer emails. In the end, my tutor phoned someone she knew, and I got a place straight away. Ravi: Lucky you. At least the cost wasn't a problem for me. The project paid for my accommodation, and I got a lift there with another student. Ella: Same here. And four weeks was just the right length. So what did you find? Ravi: Well, mostly bits of animal bone and some very ordinary pottery. I was hoping to find a coin, but no one on the whole site found one. But on my last week I found a small piece of a pot with a few letters scratched into it. The director thought it might be part of the owner's name. I was so pleased, I think I talked about it for days. Ella: That's amazing. I didn't find anything as exciting as that. My site was on the edge of a town, and it was being excavated because a supermarket is going to be built there. So we had to work quite fast, before the builders moved in. Ravi: Had anyone dug there before? Ella: No, nobody knew there was anything there until a survey was done for the planning application. Everyone thought it was just an old farm field. Ravi: So what did you find in the end? Ella: The remains of a Roman house, with part of a mosaic floor. The developers have agreed to change their plans slightly, so that it can be preserved under the car park. Ravi: Interesting. What did you think about the way they recorded the finds? I was surprised how strict they were. Ella: So was I. I'd assumed that taking photographs was enough, but they still wanted drawings as well. And they were very clear that you must record the exact position of an object before you lift it out of the ground. Once it's moved, that information is lost for ever. Ravi: Yes, my supervisor said exactly the same thing. Did you do any finds washing? Ella: Oh, don't remind me. I did something really stupid. I was given a tray of finds to wash, and I didn't read the label properly. It said that some of the seeds in it were burnt and mustn't be washed, because they were going to be sent to a lab. I washed the lot. Luckily, there were plenty more samples. Ravi: Oh no. Well, at least you didn't break anything. Did your supervisor say anything about volunteers? Mine had some strong views on that. Ella: Mine too. She said that a lot of the work they pay specialists to do, like sorting pottery, could easily be done by volunteers with a bit of guidance. Ravi: That's exactly what my supervisor said. She thought there were plenty of volunteers, but they weren't being given enough responsibility. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Ella: Anyway, we need to choose our modules for next year. What did you think of the ones we did last term? Ravi: Well, I was dreading the dating techniques module, because there was so much chemistry involved. But actually, once the lecturer explained how radiocarbon dating works, it all made sense, and I got a good mark in the exam. Ella: I found the reading for that one really heavy going, though. All those chapters on tree rings. What about human remains? Ravi: That was the one that really affected me. I had no idea how many skeletons from medieval cemeteries show signs of serious injury. Nearly all the adults seemed to have broken bones. I found that quite disturbing. Ella: Yes, it certainly makes you realise how hard life was. And ancient trade? Ravi: That was interesting, but what struck me was how many basic questions haven't been answered yet. Ella: I felt exactly the same. We know goods like amber travelled right across Europe, but nobody really knows how, or who was carrying them. I was amazed there's so little research on it. Ravi: And what about underwater archaeology? You seemed to love that. Ella: I did. The lectures weren't very well organised, and the reading list was far too long, but I've already started looking at master's courses in it. I'd really like to learn to dive and work on shipwrecks. Ravi: Well, you'd better start swimming lessons, then. Ella: Very funny. Actually, I'm quite a good swimmer. Anyway, shall we meet on Friday and go through the options for next year together? Ravi: Good idea. I'll bring the course handbook, and we can make a list. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student giving a presentation on the history of kites. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation today, I'm going to talk about kites. Most of us think of them as toys, something you fly on the beach on a windy afternoon. But kites have a long and surprisingly serious history, and they've played a part in science, warfare and religion in many parts of the world. I became interested in the subject last year, when I visited a kite museum in Japan and was amazed by how many different traditions there are. Student: Kites were almost certainly first made in China, over two thousand years ago. According to tradition, the very first ones were made of wood, but they soon came to be made from silk stretched over a frame of bamboo, both of which were widely available in China. And they weren't used for fun. The military used them to send signals between groups of soldiers, and there are even stories of kites being used to measure the distance to an enemy's walls. In some parts of Indonesia, a very different tradition developed. There, kites were made from leaves, and fishermen flew them over the sea with a line and bait hanging down into the water. This method is still used today in some places, and some researchers believe the tradition may be even older than the Chinese one, although there is little evidence to prove it. Student: Kites also played an important role in the history of science. The most famous example is probably Benjamin Franklin, who in seventeen fifty-two is said to have flown a kite in a thunderstorm to show that lightning was a form of electricity. It was a very dangerous thing to do, and some later scientists who tried to repeat it were killed. Historians still argue about whether Franklin really carried out the experiment in the way he described. At the end of the nineteenth century, an Australian inventor called Lawrence Hargrave developed the box kite, which was much more stable than earlier designs. He even lifted himself off the ground using four of them tied together. A few years later, the Wright brothers used kites to test their ideas about the design of wings, before they built their first powered aircraft. And for about forty years, weather services in several countries used kites to carry instruments high into the sky, to measure the air temperature and the speed of the wind. This continued until aircraft and balloons took over the job in the nineteen thirties. Student: Kites are also an important part of many cultures. In the Indian state of Gujarat, a huge kite festival is held every January to mark the end of winter. It lasts two days, and many families spend almost the whole time on their rooftops. In recent years, it has also attracted visitors from all over the world. The sky over cities like Ahmedabad is filled with kites, and people compete to cut each other's strings. To make this possible, the strings are coated with a mixture of glue and powdered glass. Sadly, this causes many injuries to birds, and in some places the most dangerous types of string have now been banned. Student: In Guatemala, on the first of November, people in some towns fly enormous, brightly coloured kites in the cemeteries. Some of these are several metres across, and they can take months to make. Their designs often include messages about social issues, as well as traditional patterns. The kites are believed to carry messages to the dead, and to help families feel close to relatives they have lost. Student: Finally, kites can have political meaning too. In Afghanistan, kite flying has been a popular pastime for centuries, and kite fighting is a traditional sport. As in India, the aim is to cut your opponent's string, and children race through the streets to catch the kites that have been cut loose. But during the years when the Taliban were in power in the late nineteen nineties, kite flying was banned, along with many other forms of entertainment. When that period ended, one of the first things people did was fly their kites again. Many people know this story from the novel The Kite Runner. So, as you can see, kites are much more than toys. In the second part of my talk, I'd like to look at how they're being used today, including some recent experiments using kites to generate electricity. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
